extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing and prosecuting patent claim definiteness under 35 U.S.C. 112(b)/pre‑AIA 112, second paragraph, covering correspondence between claims and specification, terminology, numerical ranges, antecedent basis, interview practice, and file history. Intended to direct examiners (and advise applicants) on when to object or reject and how to document and resolve issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete file history reflecting reasons for allowance
rubrics_metrics.description: The file history should clearly reflect the reasons why the application was allowed and should be complete so the record 'speaks for itself.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must ensure the file history is complete to facilitate evaluation of patent scope and strength and to help avoid or simplify subsequent litigation. See MPEP § 1302.14, subsection I. When allowing a claim based on an interpretation not readily apparent from prosecution, set forth in the reasons for allowance the claim interpretation applied (especially after an interview). Ensure reasons do not place unwarranted interpretations, broad or narrow, upon the claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use interviews to resolve indefiniteness and document substance
rubrics_metrics.description: When indefiniteness is the only issue, attempt resolution through an interview before issuing a rejection; the substance of any interview must be made of record in the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interviews are encouraged at any point if they further prosecution, shorten pendency, or provide benefit. Examiners may initiate interviews to discuss broadest reasonable interpretation, meaning of particular limitations, scope/clarity of preamble, intended use language, and means-plus-function limitations. Regardless of outcome, the substance (matters discussed, reasons, any agreements) must be entered into the record. See MPEP § 713.04 and 37 CFR 1.2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make of record specific 35 U.S.C. 112 issues discussed in interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of 35 U.S.C. 112 issues that should be made of record after an interview include why a term is or is not sufficiently clear, inconsistency with the specification, whether 112(f) is invoked and corresponding structure identification, and any claim amendments discussed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document why a term is/is not clear; why it is/is not inconsistent with the specification; whether it invokes 35 U.S.C. 112(f) (pre‑AIA 112, sixth paragraph) and, if so, identify corresponding structure/material/acts in the specification; record any claim amendments proposed to resolve ambiguities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification should serve as a glossary; claim terms need clear support/antecedent basis
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification should ideally serve as a glossary to the claim terms so that the examiner and the public can clearly ascertain the meaning of the claim terms; claim terms must find clear support or antecedent basis in the specification per 37 CFR 1.75(d)(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification does not provide needed support or antecedent basis, object under 37 CFR 1.75(d)(1) and require applicant to amend the description or claims (without introducing new matter). Glossaries in the spec are a helpful device. See MPEP § 608.01(o) and § 2181, subsection IV.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid internal inconsistencies between claims and specification or among claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim may be indefinite when a conflict or inconsistency between the claimed subject matter and the specification disclosure renders the scope of the claim uncertain, or when inconsistencies among claims render scope uncertain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine for internal inconsistency examples (cases cited such as In re Cohn, In re Anderson, and Tvngo Ltd. v. LG Elecs.). Dependent claims that contradict independent claims can make the disputed phrase indefinite. Consider specification, other claims, and prosecution history to clarify meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth is not indefiniteness
rubrics_metrics.description: A broad claim is not indefinite merely because it encompasses a wide scope, provided the scope is clearly defined; indefiniteness arises when boundaries are not clearly delineated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish undue breadth from indefiniteness. If claim is too broad because it does not set forth what the inventor regards as the invention, consider rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b). If too broad for lack of support/enabling disclosure, consider 35 U.S.C. 112(a). If too broad because it reads on the prior art, consider 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of every term should be apparent at filing
rubrics_metrics.description: The meaning of every term used in a claim should be apparent from the prior art or from the specification and drawings at the time the application is filed; claim language must not be 'ambiguous, vague, incoherent, opaque, or otherwise unclear.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims are given the broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification during examination. Applicants may use new terminology, but terms must be made clear and precise so the metes and bounds of the claimed invention can be ascertained. When the specification states the intended meaning, examine using that definition (cases: Packard, Morris, Prater, Zletz).

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance requirement for clarity with language and science limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: The requirement for clarity and precision must be balanced with the limitations of the language and the science; claims should be as precise as the subject matter permits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New terms are permissible and often desirable, particularly for evolving technologies. If language is not as precise as subject matter permits, the examiner should provide reasons for indefiniteness and suggest alternatives that would avoid rejection (Packard). The standard is reasonable precision in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terms used contrary to ordinary meaning must be redefined in the written description
rubrics_metrics.description: If an applicant uses a term contrary to its ordinary meaning, the written description must clearly redefine the term so as to put one skilled in the art on notice of the redefinition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant may act as own lexicographer, but the written description must clearly redefine the claim term (cases: Process Control Corp. v. HydReclaim; Hormone Research Foundation v. Genentech). Until redefinition is clear, a 112(b) rejection is appropriate; consult technical dictionaries where relevant (MPEP § 2111.01).

rubrics_metrics.name: Terms of degree require a standard for measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of terms of degree (relative terminology) is not necessarily indefinite, but the examiner should determine whether the specification provides some standard for measuring that degree or whether a recognized standard in the art exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification provides examples/teachings or figures to measure the degree, the term can be definite even without precise numerical measurement (cases: Interval Licensing v. AOL, Hearing Components v. Shure, Enzo Biochem). If no standard is provided, consider whether one skilled in the art could nevertheless ascertain the scope. Applicants may overcome rejections by submitting evidence (e.g., declarations under 37 CFR 1.132).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to a variable object or undefined positional relationships may render claim indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that define limitations by reference to an object whose relationship is not sufficiently defined (e.g., positional relationships to a user of unspecified height) may be indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When elements have two or more plausible constructions and the examiner cannot ascertain positional relationships, the claim may be indefinite (cases: Ex parte Miyazaki, Ex parte Brummer). By contrast, 'so dimensioned as to be insertable through the space between the doorframe of an automobile and one of the seats' was definite (Orthokinetics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximations like 'about' must be interpreted in context
rubrics_metrics.description: Determining the range encompassed by the term 'about' requires consideration of the context in the specification and claims; 'about' may be definite or indefinite depending on the disclosure and prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a stretch rate 'exceeding about 10% per second' was definite because measurable; 'at least about' was held indefinite where close prior art and no guidance existed (W.L. Gore; Amgen v. Chugai). Examine whether the specification gives guidance to measure the approximation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Essentially', 'substantially', and similar approximative terms must have guidelines in the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases such as 'essentially free of', 'substantially', or 'essentially' can be definite if the specification contains guidelines or examples allowing PHOSITA to draw boundaries; absent such guidance they may be indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'essentially free of alkali metal' was definite when guidelines enabled line-drawing between unavoidable impurities and essential ingredients (In re Marosi). 'Substantially' has been held definite when general guidelines are present (In re Nehrenberg, In re Mattison).

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Similar' and 'type' can render claims indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of terms like 'similar' (e.g., 'or similar apparatus') and the addition of 'type' to otherwise definite expressions can extend scope and render the claim indefinite if intended scope is unclear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'similar apparatus' was held indefinite (Ex parte Kristensen); 'ZSM-5-type' aluminosilicate zeolites held indefinite where 'type' was unclear and dependent claims fell outside the genus (Ex parte Attig).

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjective terms require an objective standard in the specification
rubrics_metrics.description: When a subjective term is used in the claim (e.g., 'aesthetically pleasing', 'comparable', 'superior'), the examiner should determine whether the specification supplies an objective standard for measuring the term; otherwise the claim may be indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim scope cannot depend solely on the unrestrained subjective opinion of an individual. If no objective boundary is provided, rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) is appropriate (Datamize; Interval Licensing). Applicants may overcome by amending or providing evidence that PHOSITA can ascertain the meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid putting both narrow and broader numerical ranges in the same claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a narrow numerical range that falls within a broader range in the same claim may render the claim indefinite when the boundaries are not discernible (e.g., 'between 45 and 78 C, preferably between 50 and 60 C').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferences and examples belong in the specification or in dependent claims. If it is unclear whether the narrower range is a limitation, make a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(b). Dependent claims narrowing a range from an independent claim are acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open-ended numerical ranges should be analyzed for definiteness
rubrics_metrics.description: Open-ended ranges (e.g., 'at least 20% sodium') must be checked for internal consistency with other claim language (e.g., dependent claims that sum to 100% excluding the 'at least' component).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze percent bases and inclusivity. A theoretical >100% content across components is not per se indefinite. Consider whether the claim meaning is clear in context (cases: In re Kroekel, In re Kirsch, In re Mochel).

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Effective amount' depends on whether PHOSITA can determine values from disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: The phrase 'an effective amount' may be definite if one skilled in the art could determine specific values based on the disclosure (examples, guidelines); otherwise it may be indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the specification and examples give guidance enabling one of ordinary skill to determine amounts (In re Halleck), treat as definite. If the function to be achieved is not stated or multiple effects could be implied, it may be indefinite (In re Fredericksen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples or preferences ('for example', 'such as') belong in the specification, not claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Description of examples or preferences should be in the specification rather than the claims; if stated in claims, they may lead to confusion over intended scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mere use of 'such as' or 'for example' in a claim does not by itself render it indefinite, but many fact-specific examples (listed in MPEP) have been held indefinite. Use caution and analyze whether the example in the claim is being used as a limitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide antecedent basis for claim terms; avoid unclear 'said'/'the' references
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is indefinite when it contains words or phrases whose meaning is unclear because there is no earlier recitation or it is unclear which previous element is being referenced (lack of antecedent basis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If 'said lever' or 'the lever' lacks earlier recitation, the claim may be indefinite. However, failure to provide explicit antecedent basis does not always render a claim indefinite if the scope is reasonably ascertainable by PHOSITA (Ex parte Porter). Inherent components have antecedent basis in recited elements (Bose v. JBL). Examiners should suggest corrections to antecedent problems.
